title: Jonang and the Rime movement
hook: smaller schools like Jonang, and the nineteenth-century movement that honored all lineages without bias

segments.voice: Yesterday, monastic study: the courtyard, the clap, the long road to the geshe degree. Your line was years of study. Did you give twenty minutes to one hard thing? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

This week: Sakya and Gelug. Last week: Nyingma and Kagyu. Big names, big monasteries. It would be easy to think that's the whole map. It isn't. Tibet also held smaller lineages, some with brilliant teachers and unusual ideas, some kept alive by a handful of monasteries far from the center. Small things are easy to lose. A dialect only a few old people still speak. A song that only one village sings. In eastern Tibet, a circle of teachers looked at all the lineages around them and decided not to let any of them quietly disappear. What they started is called Rime.
screen: `THE BIG SCHOOLS AREN'T THE WHOLE MAP.` → `SMALL THINGS ARE EASY TO LOSE.` → `RIME.`

segments.voice: First, one of the smaller schools: Jonang. Its great teacher Dolpopa taught a view often called empty of other. Emptiness, as earlier lessons put it, means things are empty of a fixed self of their own. Dolpopa taught that ultimate reality, the Buddha nature, is not empty of itself. It is empty only of everything that isn't it, like a clear sky that is empty of clouds but not empty of being sky. Other Tibetan teachers argued hard against this view, and the Jonang school was pushed to the edges for a long time. It survived, and its monasteries still teach today. Second, the word Rime. It's said REE-may, and it means without sides, or without bias. It isn't a new school. It's a way of standing toward all the schools. Third, the people. In eastern Tibet, teachers remembered as Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Jamgon Kongtrul traveled to receive teachings from every lineage they could find, large and small, including Jonang. Kongtrul gathered what they received into great written collections so the teachings would not be lost. They didn't erase the differences between schools. They kept each one, with its own flavor, and studied each one on its own terms. Fourth, what without bias means. It doesn't mean every view is the same. Rime teachers still had their own home lineages and their own convictions. It means you can hold your own way firmly and still honor someone else's, receive it carefully, and want it to survive. That's harder than agreeing with everyone, and it's harder than dismissing them.
screen: `JONANG: EMPTY OF OTHER.` · `RIME: WITHOUT SIDES.` · `KHYENTSE AND KONGTRUL GATHER EVERY LINEAGE.` · `YOUR OWN WAY, AND HONOR FOR THEIRS.` · then, large: `WITHOUT BIAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a tradition not your own. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one tradition, religious or not, that isn't yours: a neighbor's faith, a grandparent's custom, a practice you've only watched from outside. Without agreeing or disagreeing, name one thing in it that you find beautiful or wise. Hold that one thing quietly, the way Kongtrul might have held a teaching he'd traveled far to receive. The bell holds the time.
Rime. Without sides, without bias: a movement in eastern Tibet to receive, honor and preserve every lineage, large and small. Today's word.
Your line: without bias. Today, when someone does a thing differently from you, ask them how they learned it before you decide what you think. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Teachers in the Rime spirit receive and pass on teachings from several Tibetan lineages while keeping their own; Jonang monasteries continue to teach Dolpopa's view and their own practice lineages.
